teaser: As a copy of a real body, he gets almost everything wrong. That was never the goal.
review_notes:
Met accession 32.11.1, Naxian marble, height about 194.6 cm, Attic, ca. 590-580 BC, said to have marked the grave of a young Athenian aristocrat (Met).
Diodorus Siculus (1.98) story of Telekles and Theodoros making a statue in two halves.
The thin lines across the torso and shins in the photo are read here as joins from reassembly; please confirm.
'Originally painted' is standard for Archaic marble; no specific pigment claim is made for this statue.

lesson.text: Judge him as a study of a living body and he fails. The eyes are too big and too flat. The shoulders are a shelf. The kneecaps look like carved ornaments, the hair like rows of beads. Nobody stands this stiffly. If a sculptor made this a century later in Athens, he would have been laughed out of the workshop.

Yet this is one of the earliest marble statues of a human being ever made in Attica, the region around Athens, around 590 BC. Its sculptor was not trying to copy a man and missing. He was solving a different problem: how to get a standing figure out of a block of stone at all.

Here is how it was done. The carver drew the figure on the four faces of the block: front, back, two sides. Then he cut straight inward from each drawing until the four views met in the middle. That method leaves a clear signature, and you can still read it.
Four lines show how strictly the block ruled the body.

lines.label: The axis
lines.text: Drop a line from the top of the skull. Nose, breastbone, navel and groin all sit on it. The left half of the body mirrors the right.

lines.label: Shoulders
lines.text: Perfectly level. In a real person who steps forward, one shoulder dips. Here nothing reacts to anything else.

lines.label: Hips
lines.text: Level again, even though one foot is advanced. He is not walking. He is a standing figure with one leg slid forward.

lines.label: The V
lines.text: The belly ends in two straight grooves. Muscles are not modeled as swelling flesh. They are drawn on the surface, like lines on a map.

lesson.text: That pose was borrowed. Greek traders and hired soldiers had been living in Egypt for decades and had seen its stone figures: left foot forward, arms at the sides, fists closed. Egyptian sculptors used a grid of fixed proportions, and Greeks seem to have taken that home too.

The ancient historian Diodorus tells of two Greek brothers, Telekles and Theodoros, who used the Egyptian system to carve the two halves of one statue in two different cities. When the halves were brought together, he says, they fit exactly.

But the Greek carver changed two things, and both were daring. Egyptian stone figures wear a kilt and lean against a slab of stone, with stone left between the legs and under the arms. This young man has been cut free of all that.

lesson.title: What Greece changed
lesson.text: Three places where the sculptor took a risk an Egyptian workshop would not.

spots.title: Daylight
spots.text: A dark gap separates arm from waist. The stone has been cut all the way through, leaving the arm attached only at the shoulder and the fist. One slip and it snaps.

spots.title: Open legs
spots.text: No stone fills the space between the shins. The whole weight of the marble stands on two ankles. He is 1.95 m tall (about 6 ft 5 in).

spots.title: Nothing to wear
spots.text: He is nude, apart from a neckband. Greek men exercised naked, and a fit bare body was a sign of excellence, not shame. Egypt never showed its nobles this way.

lesson.text: The Greeks borrowed the pose from Egypt and then removed the support. A figure that stands by itself, with air all around it, is the beginning of freestanding sculpture in Europe.

He has a name as a type: kouros, the Greek word for a youth. Hundreds were carved between about 650 and 480 BC. They are not portraits. Every kouros is the same ideal young man, beardless, long-haired, at the peak of his strength.

This one stood over a grave. He marked the burial of a young Athenian from a wealthy family, out in the countryside where passersby on the road could see him. Others were set up in sanctuaries as gifts to a god. In both cases the statue said the same thing: here was someone at his best.

The marble traveled farther than he ever would. It comes from Naxos, an island in the middle of the Aegean Sea, some 170 km (about 105 miles) by ship from Athens. A block this size weighed well over a ton before carving began.

Now that you know the rules of the game, the details stop looking like errors. Each one is a pattern, chosen and repeated with care. Wander over the figure from the top of the head down to the plinth.

spots.title: Eyes
spots.text: Large, almond-shaped and wide open, with the lids cut as sharp ridges. They were made to be read from a distance, outdoors, in hard sunlight.

spots.title: Beaded hair
spots.text: The hair falls in strings of small knobs, tied by a band. It is closer to jewelry than to hair, a pattern that catches light in rows.

spots.title: Neckband
spots.text: A thin band circles the throat, knotted at the front. It is the only thing he wears.

spots.title: Fist
spots.text: The hand is closed with the thumb forward. A scrap of stone still links it to the thigh, the last bridge the carver did not dare remove.

spots.title: Knees
spots.text: The kneecaps and the muscles above them are cut as neat symmetrical shapes, almost like a seal stamped into each leg.

spots.title: The left foot
spots.text: It is his left foot that advances, as in Egypt. Both soles stay flat on the plinth, the thin stone slab he stands on. No heel lifts.

lesson.text: Imagine him also in color. Marble statues of this period were painted: hair, eyes, lips, the band at the neck. The pale stone you see is what twenty-six centuries of weather and burial have left.
He reached New York in 1932. The thin lines you can spot across his body are breaks: the statue came out of the ground in pieces and was put back together.

Within about a hundred years, Greek sculptors would let the hips tilt, the shoulders answer, the weight settle on one leg. Every one of those later, relaxed bodies starts from this rigid one. He is the fixed point they learned to move away from.

quiz.question: What does the word kouros mean?
quiz.explanation: Kouros is the Greek word for a youth, and names this type of statue.

quiz.question: Which culture's statues inspired the pose?
quiz.explanation: Left foot forward, arms down and fists closed come from Egyptian stone figures.

quiz.question: What did the Greek sculptor remove that Egyptian statues kept?
options: The supporting stone behind the figure and between the limbs
quiz.explanation: The kouros is cut free, with open space between arms, legs and body.

quiz.question: What was this statue used for?
options: It marked the grave of a young Athenian
It held up a temple roof
quiz.explanation: It stood over the burial of a young man from a wealthy family.

quiz.question: How did the carver begin?
options: By modeling the figure in clay and casting it
By drawing the figure on the four faces of the block
By copying a living model limb by limb
quiz.explanation: He drew four views on the block and cut inward from each.

facts.text: The kouros is a portrait of a specific, recognizable man.
facts.explanation: Kouroi show an ideal youth, not an individual likeness.

facts.text: The marble was quarried on the island of Naxos.
facts.explanation: The stone was shipped across the Aegean from Naxos to Attica.

facts.text: Statues like this were left as bare white marble on purpose.
facts.explanation: They were painted; the color has worn away over the centuries.
